cards.t: Systolic versus diastolic murmurs (timing comes first)
q: how do I tell if a murmur is systolic or diastolic
what do I ask when I hear a murmur
why feel the carotid while listening
cards.x:
The first job with any murmur is deciding when it happens. A systolic murmur falls between S1 (the first heart sound) and S2 (the second heart sound). A diastolic murmur falls between S2 and the next S1.

If you cannot tell which gap you are hearing, feel the carotid artery in the neck while you listen. Systolic sounds line up with the upstroke of the carotid pulse, so a murmur that lands with the pulse is systolic.

Once the timing is settled, name where it sits. Systolic murmurs are midsystolic, pansystolic (also called holosystolic) or late systolic. Diastolic murmurs are early, mid or late, and they are less common and harder to hear than systolic ones. Ask the same questions every time: systole or diastole, how long, where is it loudest and does it radiate, crescendo or decrescendo, and are there any extra heart sounds?

cards.t: Extra sounds paired with their murmurs
q: which extra heart sounds go with which murmurs
what murmur follows an opening snap
why is an S3 heard with a holosystolic murmur
cards.x:
Some extra sounds and murmurs come as pairs because one condition causes both.

- Mitral valve prolapse: a mid to late systolic click, then a late systolic murmur from mitral regurgitation that builds up to the second heart sound.
- An S3 (the third heart sound) with a holosystolic murmur: mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur. The ventricular volume overload it causes is one cause of an S3.
- An S4 (the fourth heart sound) with a midsystolic murmur: aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are causes of an S4. Both are midsystolic murmurs.
- Opening snap with a diastolic murmur: a stenotic mitral valve opens with a high-pitched snap (heard with the diaphragm). The low-pitched mid to late diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis follows it, heard with the bell at the apex.
- Ejection sound with a midsystolic murmur: a pulmonic ejection sound is high pitched and comes right after the first heart sound. Pulmonic stenosis is one cause of it. Its murmur is midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, at the pulmonic area.

Listen for the two things separately: the extra sound, then the murmur.

cards.t: Special maneuvers: preload, afterload and three murmurs
k: Valsalva standing squatting hand grip leg raise
q: what do special maneuvers do to murmurs
what is preload and afterload
which murmurs do the maneuvers help separate
cards.x:
Special maneuvers are simple changes in position or effort that make a murmur louder or softer by changing the load on the heart. Each one changes either how much blood returns to the heart (preload) or how hard the heart has to pump against (afterload). That changes how loud the murmur is.

There are five: Valsalva, standing, squatting, raised legs while lying supine, and sustained hand grip. They are tracked against three conditions: aortic stenosis, mitral valve prolapse and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

The reason to learn them is that murmurs that sound alike separate when you change filling and resistance. Learn the directions as a pattern. The aortic stenosis murmur and the hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy murmur usually move in opposite directions. The mitral valve prolapse murmur moves with the hypertrophic one.

cards.t: How maneuvers change aortic stenosis, prolapse and hypertrophic murmurs
k: Valsalva standing squatting raised legs hand grip table
aortic stenosis versus hypertrophic cardiomyopathy maneuvers
q: how do the maneuvers change aortic stenosis versus hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
what does squatting do to a murmur
which murmurs move in opposite directions with maneuvers
cards.x:
Across the five maneuvers, the aortic stenosis murmur and the hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy murmur mostly move in opposite directions. The mitral valve prolapse murmur follows the hypertrophic one.

- Valsalva and standing both decrease preload. They decrease the aortic stenosis murmur and increase the mitral valve prolapse and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy murmurs.
- Squatting and raised legs, lying supine, both increase preload. They do the reverse: they increase the aortic stenosis murmur and decrease the mitral valve prolapse and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy murmurs.
- Standing also decreases afterload (the resistance the heart pumps against). Squatting increases it.

So aortic stenosis and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy move in opposite directions on Valsalva, standing, squatting and raised legs. On those four, mitral valve prolapse always moves the same way as hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Sustained hand grip is the odd one out: it raises afterload and makes the aortic stenosis and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy murmurs softer.

cards.t: The path of blood through the heart and its valves
q: what order does blood cross the heart valves
which valve does blood cross first
why do I need to know the blood flow pathway
cards.x:
Blood follows one fixed route. Oxygen-poor blood returns from the body through the inferior and superior vena cava into the right atrium. It crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The ventricle pumps it through the pulmonic valve into the pulmonary artery and on to the lungs. It returns through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve into the aorta and the rest of the body.

The tricuspid is the first valve blood crosses on its way back to the heart. A memory trick is 'try before you buy': tricuspid comes before bicuspid, which is the mitral valve.

Know this route cold, because every murmur is read off it. A valve may be narrowed or leaking, or there may be an extra pathway that should not exist. Then blood no longer flows the way you expect, and that change is what you hear.

cards.t: The angle of Louis and counting intercostal spaces
q: what is the angle of Louis
how do I find the second intercostal space
how do I count down to the fifth intercostal space
cards.x:
The angle of Louis is the sternal-manubrial junction. That is the joint where the top piece of the breastbone (the manubrium) meets the rest of it. It lies beside the second rib, so the second intercostal space (the gap between ribs) sits directly below it.

That makes it your starting point for counting. Find the angle, drop into the second space, then count down rib space by rib space. Counting down to the fifth space takes you to where the apex of the heart is found.

This matters because the listening areas for the heart sit at named rib spaces beside the sternum and at the apex. The point of maximal impulse is normally in the fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the left midclavicular line. If you cannot find your landmarks by counting, you cannot say where a sound or murmur is loudest.

cards.t: Which part of the heart sits at the front of the chest
k: why the point of maximal impulse marks the left border
q: which ventricle is at the front of the chest
why does the point of maximal impulse mark the left border of the heart
why does the apical impulse move when the heart enlarges
cards.x:
The right ventricle makes up most of the front of the heart. The left ventricle only reaches the chest wall at its lower left tip, and that tip is what you feel as the apical impulse.

That one fact explains two things. First, the point of maximal impulse marks the heart's left border: it is the left ventricle's tip touching the chest wall. Second, it moves when the left ventricle enlarges, because a bigger left ventricle pushes that tip outward, so the impulse shifts from where it normally sits.

So when you document where you find the impulse, you are really marking where the left edge of the heart is.

cards.t: Chest pain: what to consider and how to ask
q: what should I think of with chest pain
how do women present differently with heart attack symptoms
how do I take a history of chest pain
cards.x:
Chest pain is the most common symptom of coronary artery disease (blocked or narrowed arteries feeding the heart muscle), so the heart is the first place to look. Always consider angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, dissecting aortic aneurysm and pulmonary embolism. You also have to tell cardiovascular causes apart from disorders of the pericardium, trachea, bronchi, parietal pleura, esophagus, chest wall, gallbladder, stomach and neck. Anything in that area can cause pain, but the cardiac cause is the big one to worry about first.

Men and women with acute coronary syndrome most often describe classic chest pressure or pain. It can come on with exertion or at rest. But women over 65 are likely to report atypical symptoms: upper back, neck or jaw pain, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting or fatigue. Another is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (sudden shortness of breath that wakes the patient from sleep). Keep a high index of suspicion, because an atypical symptom as ordinary as fatigue can be the way it shows up.

To take the history, begin with open-ended questions. Then ask for details, then ask the patient to point to the pain. After that ask the usual pain questions: where, radiation, severity out of ten, constant or intermittent, and character.

cards.t: Levine's sign: how the patient points to the pain
q: what is Levine's sign
why ask the patient to show where the pain is
is Levine's sign the same as the Levine grading scale
cards.x:
Levine's sign is a clenched fist held against the center of the chest when a patient is asked to show where the pain is. It is a warning sign: that gesture sets off alarm bells that this is the real deal.

How a patient points is itself a finding. A vague burning line up the middle of the chest points toward the esophagus, and a single fingertip points toward a rib or muscle. Even then it could still be cardiac, so you do not simply write it off.

Do not confuse it with the Levine grading system, which is the six-point scale used to grade how loud a murmur is. The sign is a gesture; the grading system is a loudness scale.

cards.t: Palpitations and how to ask about them
q: what are palpitations
do palpitations always mean heart disease
what questions do I ask about palpitations
cards.x:
Palpitations are an unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat. Patients describe them as skipping, racing, fluttering, pounding or stopping of the heart. The heartbeat may be irregular, may speed up or slow down rapidly, or may simply feel more forceful.

They do not necessarily mean heart disease: anxious patients and hyperthyroid patients may report them.

Patients do not always use the word, so reword the question. Ask: Are you aware of your heartbeat? What does it feel like? Fast? Slow? Regular? Irregular? How long does it last? After the history, get an electrocardiogram.

cards.t: Dyspnea, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
q: what is the difference between dyspnea, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
how do I quantify orthopnea
is orthopnea always cardiac
cards.x:
These are three ways of describing shortness of breath, and the difference is mostly about timing and position.

- Dyspnea: an uncomfortable awareness of breathing that is out of proportion to the level of exertion. It is common in both cardiac and pulmonary problems, so relate it to what the patient can still do day to day.
- Orthopnea: dyspnea when lying flat that improves when sitting up. Quantify it by the number of pillows used for sleeping, or the need to sleep sitting up, and ask what the pillows are for.
- Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: sudden dyspnea and orthopnea that awaken the patient from sleep, usually 1 to 2 hours after going to bed. The patient sits up, stands up or goes to the window for air, and there may be wheezing and coughing.

Orthopnea is not only cardiac; it can be pulmonary or even abdominal.

cards.t: Asking about swelling, and why daily weight helps
q: what do I ask a patient about swelling
why recommend a daily morning weight
what is dry weight
cards.x:
Edema is excessive fluid in the extravascular interstitial space, the tissue outside the blood vessels. Up to 10% of body weight can build up before pitting edema appears, which is why you cannot rely on your eyes alone.

Focus your questions on location, timing, setting and associated symptoms: swelling anywhere, and where else? Worse in the morning or the evening? Do your shoes get tight? Rings tight on your fingers? Eyelids puffy in the morning? Clothes tight in the middle?

Also consider recommending a daily morning weight. Weight shows edema before the eye does: a gain of two pounds overnight is not muscle or fat, it is water, so weight can signal fluid before the patient looks puffy or has pitting. Dialysis and heart failure patients should know their dry weight, their weight at fluid balance, so a rise from it can be caught.

cards.t: Fainting (syncope): the clues before and after
q: what is syncope
how do I tell the cause of fainting from the history
what are the most common causes of syncope
cards.x:
Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness followed by recovery. The most common cause is neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope, and about 20% of cases are of cardiac origin from arrhythmias. Ask whether the patient felt faint, felt about to fall or pass out, or felt unsteady and off balance.

The history before and after the faint is often more valuable than the spell itself, and it points to the cause:

- Lightheaded, pale and clammy first, often with a trigger: vasovagal.
- Stood up from a crouch, tunnel vision, then down: orthostatic.
- Sudden, with no warning: think arrhythmia. This can be an emergency; if the patient does not wake promptly or has no pulse, get a defibrillator and call 911.
- Comes round agitated and confused: a postictal phase, so think seizure.

A useful piece of patient education: if you feel faint, sit down, wherever you are.

cards.t: The cardiac cycle: systole, diastole and which valves are open
k: which valves are open in systole
q: what is the cardiac cycle
which valves are open in systole and diastole
what makes the first and second heart sounds
cards.x:
The cardiac cycle is the time from the start of one heartbeat to the start of the next: contraction alternating with relaxation. Systole and diastole are both named for what the ventricles are doing.

In systole, ventricular pressure is higher than atrial pressure. The mitral and tricuspid valves (the atrioventricular valves, helped by the papillary muscles) close. The aortic and pulmonic valves open, so the right ventricle ejects into the pulmonary artery and the left into the aorta. The mitral and tricuspid closing makes the first heart sound, the 'lub'.

In diastole, ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure. The aortic and pulmonic valves close, which makes the second heart sound, the 'dub'. The mitral and tricuspid valves open, so the atria empty into the ventricles. Systole is the shorter interval and diastole the longer one.

cards.t: The first and second heart sounds (S1 and S2) compared
q: what is the difference between S1 and S2
where do I listen for S1 and S2
how do I tell S1 from S2 with the carotid pulse
cards.x:
S1 (the first heart sound) is the 'lub': closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves. S2 (the second heart sound) is the 'dub': closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves.

- Best heard: both with the diaphragm, S1 at the apex and S2 at the base.
- Splitting: S1 is usually not split. S2 can be heard split, at Erb's point and the pulmonic area, and normal splitting is best heard at the pulmonic area.
- Against the carotid pulse: S1 comes just before it and S2 comes just after it. That is a handy way to tell which sound you are on if the rhythm is hard to follow.

Everything else you hear is placed relative to these two. Systole sits between S1 and S2, and diastole sits between S2 and the next S1.

cards.t: Splitting of the second heart sound: physiologic versus pathologic
q: what is physiologic splitting of S2
when is a split S2 abnormal
why does S2 split on inspiration
cards.x:
The second heart sound has two parts: A2 (the aortic component), usually louder because of the high pressure in the aorta, and P2 (the pulmonic component). There are always two sounds. The only question is whether they land on top of each other or apart.

Normally they are fused into one sound during expiration and audibly separate during inspiration. That is physiologic splitting, and it is normal. On full inspiration P2 comes a little later, so the two parts land apart; on full expiration they land together. The split comes and goes with breathing, and a single second sound is just the fused version heard on expiration.

If you can still hear two sounds during expiration, that is pathologic splitting and suggests heart disease. A pathologic split stays audible when the breath is out; the classic example is a fixed split, which does not change with breathing. The test is simple: listen with the breath fully out.

cards.t: Early ejection sound
q: what is an early ejection sound
how do I tell an aortic from a pulmonic ejection sound
what causes an ejection sound
cards.x:
An early ejection sound is a high-pitched, sharp clicking sound heard shortly after the first heart sound. It is the sound of the aortic or pulmonic valve halting suddenly and abnormally as it opens at the start of systole. It is best heard with the diaphragm, and it indicates cardiovascular disease.

Where it is heard separates the two types:

- Aortic: heard at the base and the apex, does not change with inspiration. Causes include a dilated aorta and aortic valve disease from congenital stenosis or a bicuspid valve.
- Pulmonic: best in the second and third intercostal spaces, and it decreases with inspiration. Causes include a dilated pulmonary artery, pulmonary hypertension and pulmonic stenosis.

Quick way to tell it from a click: an ejection sound comes right after the first heart sound, while a click comes in mid to late systole.

cards.t: Systolic click and mitral valve prolapse
q: what is a systolic click
what causes a mid-systolic click
what murmur follows a click
cards.x:
A systolic click is a high-pitched sound in mid to late systole. It is best heard with the diaphragm at or medial to the apex and along the lower left sternal border. It is usually a single click, but there may be several.

It is usually caused by mitral valve prolapse, where part of the mitral valve balloons back into the left atrium during systole. The click is then followed by a late systolic murmur from mitral regurgitation. This murmur builds (crescendos) up to the second heart sound.

So the classic pattern of prolapse is: click first, then a late systolic murmur that gets louder toward the second heart sound. Quick way to tell the click from an ejection sound: the ejection sound comes right after the first heart sound, while the click comes later, in mid to late systole.

cards.t: S3, the ventricular gallop
q: what is an S3 heart sound
when is an S3 normal and when is it abnormal
how do I listen for an S3
cards.x:
S3 (the third heart sound) comes just after the second heart sound, early in diastole. Its cadence is lub-dub-dee, like the word Kentucky with the stress on the middle syllable. It is low pitched, so listen with the bell at the apex, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.

Age decides whether it matters. An S3 is normal in children and young adults (up to 35 to 40) and in the last trimester of pregnancy. In adults over 40 it is pathologic, because it reflects high left ventricular filling pressures and abrupt deceleration of inflow across the mitral valve at the end of rapid filling, the blood slapping against the left ventricular wall.

Causes in adults include decreased contractility, heart failure, volume overload from aortic or mitral regurgitation, and left-to-right shunts.

cards.t: S4, the atrial gallop
q: what is an S4 heart sound
what causes an S4
when is an S4 normal
cards.x:
S4 (the fourth heart sound) comes just before the first heart sound, late in diastole. Its cadence is dee-lub-dub, like the word Tennessee with the stress on the last syllable. It is dull and low pitched, so use the bell at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. A right-sided one is heard at the lower left sternal border.

It is normal in trained athletes and older age groups.

When it is pathologic, it comes from a stiff ventricle. Hypertrophy or fibrosis reduces compliance (stretchiness) as the ventricle fills after the atria contract. Causes include hypertensive heart disease, aortic stenosis, ischemic and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and delayed atrioventricular conduction.

Quick way to keep the gallops straight: the third sound comes after the second heart sound and is normal in the young, while the fourth comes before the first heart sound and is normal in athletes and older people.

cards.t: The opening snap (mitral stenosis)
q: what is an opening snap
how do I tell an opening snap from an S3
why is the opening snap heard in mitral stenosis
cards.x:
An opening snap is a very early diastolic sound, right after the second heart sound, made by a stenotic (narrowed) mitral valve snapping open. The valve is stiff, so the leaflets stop abruptly as they open. It is never normal, and it becomes less audible as the leaflets calcify.

It is high pitched with an obvious snap, so use the diaphragm, just medial to the apex and along the lower left sternal border. A snap loud enough to radiate to the pulmonic area can be mistaken for the pulmonic component of the second sound; the high pitch and obvious snap are what separate it.

Quick way to tell it from S3 (the third heart sound): both sit early in diastole, but the snap is high pitched (diaphragm) and S3 is low pitched (bell). The snap is then followed by the low-pitched mid to late diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis, best heard with the bell at the apex.

cards.t: Placing the extra heart sounds in the cycle
k: how to remember the extra heart sounds
timing of ejection sound click snap S3 S4
q: in what order do the extra heart sounds occur
how do I figure out which extra sound I am hearing
how do I memorize all the heart sounds
cards.x:
A good way to keep the extra heart sounds straight is to learn them by where they fall in the cycle rather than as a flat list. Place the sound in the cycle, then ask which valves are open or shut at that moment.

Through one beat the order is:

- The first heart sound, then in systole an early ejection sound right after it, or a click in mid to late systole.
- The second heart sound, then in diastole the opening snap right after it, and S3 (the third heart sound) early in diastole.
- Late in diastole, S4 (the fourth heart sound) just before the next first heart sound.

A sound right after the first heart sound, when the aortic and pulmonic valves are opening, belongs to those valves. A snap early in diastole, when the mitral valve should be opening, suggests a stiff mitral valve opening late. Pitch separates the similar ones: the snap and ejection sound are high pitched (diaphragm), while S3 and S4 are low pitched (bell). Age helps too: S3 is normal in the young, S4 is normal in athletes and older people, and an opening snap is never normal.

cards.t: The apical impulse and the point of maximal impulse
q: what is the point of maximal impulse
where is the PMI normally
what does a displaced apical impulse mean
cards.x:
The apical impulse is the brief, early push of the left ventricle's apex against the chest wall as it contracts. You find it by feeling (palpating) the chest wall over the heart, called the precordium. The spot is recorded as the point of maximal impulse. It identifies the left border of the heart.

Normally it is in the fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the left midclavicular line. Supine, it can be about the size of a quarter (2.5 cm) and feels brisk and tapping.

A disorder can change the heart's size or shape: cardiomegaly (an enlarged heart) or hypertrophy (thickened muscle). Then the left border shifts lateral and possibly inferior, for example to the sixth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line.

One exception: in some conditions, another pulsation can be more prominent than the apex beat. Examples are right ventricular hypertrophy, a dilated pulmonary artery, aortic aneurysm, left ventricular hypertrophy or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

cards.t: Finding the apical impulse and why you document it
k: left lateral decubitus for apical impulse
document the point of maximal impulse
q: what if I cannot feel the apical impulse
how do I palpate the point of maximal impulse
why document where the apical impulse is
cards.x:
To find the impulse, start with four fingers on the chest, then lift them one at a time until a single finger sits on the most intense point.

If you cannot feel it with the patient supine, roll them into the left lateral decubitus position. Still nothing? Ask them to exhale fully and hold for a few seconds.

Always document where you actually find it, and know where it should be. A displaced impulse moves your thinking toward an enlarged heart or a shift caused by fluid in the pleural space. Muffled heart sounds with a rub point toward pericardial disease, where the impulse is often faint. Knowing where you are supposed to find it and writing down where you really find it is what makes the finding useful.

cards.t: Hyperkinetic, sustained and diffuse left ventricular impulses
q: what do hyperkinetic, sustained and diffuse mean
what causes a sustained apical impulse
how does pressure overload differ from volume overload on the impulse
cards.x:
Three words describe the left ventricular impulse, and each points to a different cause.

- Hyperkinetic: from a temporarily increased stroke volume (more blood pumped with each beat). It does not necessarily mean heart disease. Examples are anxiety, hyperthyroidism and severe anemia.
- Sustained: ventricular hypertrophy from a chronic pressure load (increased afterload, meaning the ventricle has to push against more resistance). It is larger than normal and lasts longer. Examples are aortic stenosis and hypertension.
- Diffuse: ventricular dilation from a chronic volume overload (increased preload, meaning the ventricle is filled with extra blood). It is larger than normal, spread out, displaced to the left and possibly downward. Examples are aortic or mitral regurgitation and cardiomyopathy.

The pattern to remember: a pressure load thickens the wall and sustains the impulse, while a volume load dilates the chamber and makes it diffuse and displaced. The impulse is never read alone; pair it with the rest of the exam, for example a larger, sustained impulse plus a systolic ejection murmur at the aortic area points toward aortic stenosis.

cards.t: The right ventricular impulse
q: where do I feel the right ventricular impulse
what makes the right ventricular impulse sustained
what causes a diffuse right ventricular impulse
cards.x:
The right ventricular impulse is felt at the 3rd, 4th and 5th left intercostal spaces, and possibly subxiphoid. It is much harder to distinguish than the left ventricular impulse, and its diameter is not useful.

It follows the same pattern as the left side:

- Hyperkinetic: slightly more forceful, with normal duration. The examples are the same as on the left (anxiety, hyperthyroidism, severe anemia).
- Sustained and more forceful: a pressure load on the right ventricle, as in pulmonic stenosis or pulmonary hypertension.
- Diffuse, felt at the left sternal border toward the left cardiac border and also subxiphoid, with duration normal to slightly sustained: a volume load, as in atrial septal defect.

As on the left, pressure load thickens the wall and sustains the impulse, while volume load dilates the chamber and spreads the impulse out.

cards.t: The five classic areas of auscultation
q: where are the areas of auscultation
what do I listen for at Erb's point
where is the mitral area
cards.x:
There are five classic places to listen, and each is best for certain sounds.

- Aortic: right second intercostal space at the sternal border. Aortic valve sounds, aortic stenosis and the early aortic ejection sound (with the apex).
- Pulmonic: left second intercostal space at the sternal border. Physiologic splitting of the second heart sound, the pulmonic ejection sound (second to third spaces), pulmonic stenosis and regurgitation.
- Erb's point: left third intercostal space, between the pulmonic and mitral areas. Splitting of the second sound, the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur, and most often the pericardial friction rub.
- Tricuspid: lower left sternal border. Tricuspid regurgitation and stenosis, and the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur.
- Mitral (apex): fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line. The first heart sound, the third and fourth heart sounds, and mitral regurgitation and stenosis.

cards.t: Why the listening areas are not directly over the valves
k: where each valve is versus where you listen
q: why isn't the aortic area over the aortic valve
why does an aortic stenosis murmur reach the carotids
how do I choose where to listen for each valve
cards.x:
Each listening area is not over its valve. It is the first place downstream of the valve, in the direction blood flows, where there is no bone in the way. Sound travels the same direction the blood does, so that is where it comes through to the chest wall best.

The same logic explains radiation. A loud aortic stenosis murmur can be heard in both carotid arteries, because that is where the blood goes next. So check the aortic area before deciding that what you hear in the neck is a pair of carotid bruits.

If you are ever unsure where to listen, think about the direction of blood flow past the valve. Ask where it first has a clear path to the chest wall.

cards.t: Bell versus diaphragm: which sounds each picks up
k: how to use the bell and diaphragm
q: when do I use the bell and when the diaphragm
which heart sounds are low pitched
how do I apply the bell
cards.x:
Choose the chest piece by pitch.

- Bell: picks up low-pitched sounds. Apply it lightly, with no gaps, at the apex and then moving medially along the lower sternal border. Use it for the third and fourth heart sounds and the murmur of mitral stenosis (and the tricuspid stenosis rumble).
- Diaphragm: picks up high-pitched sounds. Press it firmly and use it throughout the precordium. Use it for the first and second heart sounds, early ejection sounds, clicks, the opening snap, the murmurs of aortic and mitral regurgitation, and pericardial friction rubs.

The opening snap and the third heart sound are the pair most easily confused. Both sit early in diastole, but the snap is high pitched (diaphragm) and the third sound is low pitched (bell).

Technique: use a quiet setting, isolate each sound in turn, close your eyes to focus, and make sure the stethoscope touches the skin directly. If you hear something abnormal, stay there and listen longer.

cards.t: What a murmur is and what causes one
q: what is a heart murmur
what causes a murmur
why do children have murmurs
cards.x:
A murmur is the sound of turbulent blood flow over a heart valve, a swoosh. Smooth flow is silent; turbulence is what you hear.

Murmurs result from:

- Flow across a partially obstructed valve.
- Increased flow through a normal valve in a small child.
- Ejection into a dilated chamber.
- Regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve (one that leaks).
- Abnormal shunting of blood from one chamber to a lower pressure chamber.

Not every murmur means disease. Some are innocent or physiologic, while others are pathologic and come from a structural abnormality of the heart or great vessels.

cards.t: Thrills and bruits: the felt and vessel versions of a murmur
q: what is a thrill
what is the difference between a murmur and a bruit
how do I feel for a thrill
cards.x:
A thrill is the vibration or buzzing sensation that a murmur produces. A murmur is heard; a thrill is felt. You feel for it with the balls of your hand pressed against the chest wall and held still, most easily in the position that brings the murmur out.

A bruit is the vessel equivalent of a murmur: a murmur is to a heart valve as a bruit is to a vessel.

A good place to feel what a real thrill is like is a dialysis patient's arteriovenous fistula. If the rumble you expect there is absent, tell the nurse, because the fistula may be occluded.

A thrill also matters for grading: a palpable thrill means the murmur is at least grade 4 of 6 on the Levine scale.

cards.t: The seven features used to describe a murmur
k: timing shape location radiation intensity pitch quality
q: how do I describe a murmur
what are the features of a murmur
what is radiation of a murmur
cards.x:
A murmur is described by seven features: timing, shape, location, radiation, intensity, pitch and quality.

- Timing: systolic (between the first and second heart sounds) or diastolic (between the second and next first), and how long.
- Shape: crescendo, decrescendo, crescendo-decrescendo or plateau.
- Location: where the murmur starts, found by exploring where it is loudest. Describe it by intercostal space and distance from the sternum, or by apex, midclavicular, midsternal or axillary lines.
- Radiation: where else you hear it. It tells you about the site of origin, intensity, the direction of flow and bone conduction in the chest.
- Intensity: graded on the six-point Levine scale, written as a fraction such as 3/6.
- Pitch: high, medium or low.
- Quality: blowing, harsh, rumbling or musical.

Also check for extra heart sounds and any special tests.

cards.t: Types of murmur timing in systole and diastole
q: what is the difference between midsystolic and pansystolic murmurs
what is a continuous murmur
what does early diastolic mean
cards.x:
Murmurs are named by where they sit in the beat.

- Midsystolic: starts after the first heart sound, peaks in the middle and ends before the second. It is the diamond of the ejection murmurs.
- Pansystolic (holosystolic): starts with the first heart sound and runs all the way to the second. It is flow through something that should be shut for the whole of systole.
- Late systolic: begins after mid-systole and runs up to the second heart sound. It is the murmur that follows the click of mitral valve prolapse.
- Early diastolic: starts right after the second heart sound and fades, the decrescendo of aortic or pulmonic regurgitation.
- Mid-diastolic: starts a short time after the second sound. This is where the rumble of mitral stenosis sits.
- Late diastolic: starts late in diastole and runs up to the first heart sound.
- Continuous: starts in systole and runs through the second heart sound into diastole without stopping, so you hear it wherever you are in the cycle.

cards.t: Murmur shapes: crescendo, decrescendo, diamond and plateau
q: what does crescendo-decrescendo mean
what is a plateau murmur
what is the shape of a murmur
cards.x:
Shape is how the loudness of a murmur changes over time.

- Crescendo: grows louder.
- Decrescendo: begins at its maximum and grows silent.
- Crescendo-decrescendo: rises then falls, which makes a diamond shape. Midsystolic ejection murmurs look like this.
- Plateau: the intensity does not change. A holosystolic plateau murmur is the most precise description you can give.

Shape and timing together narrow things down quickly. For example, a late systolic murmur that builds to the second heart sound follows the click of mitral valve prolapse. An early diastolic murmur that starts loud and fades is the decrescendo of aortic or pulmonic regurgitation.

cards.t: Levine grading of murmur intensity (1 to 6)
q: how are murmurs graded
which murmur grade has a thrill
what is the difference between grade 5 and grade 6
cards.x:
Murmur loudness is graded on a six-point scale, the Levine grading system, and written as a fraction, for example 3/6.

- 1: very faint, heard only after the listener has tuned in, and may not be heard in all positions.
- 2: quiet, but heard immediately after placing the stethoscope on the chest.
- 3: moderately loud.
- 4: loud, with a palpable thrill.
- 5: very loud, with a thrill; may be heard with the stethoscope partly off the chest.
- 6: very loud, with a thrill; may be heard with the stethoscope entirely off the chest.

The hinge is grade 4, the first grade with a palpable thrill. So grading uses both the ear and the hand: how loud it is raises the grade, but when you also feel a thrill the grade jumps up to at least 4. Most murmurs seen in practice are 2s and 3s, with 4s when a thrill is present.

cards.t: Innocent, physiologic and pathologic murmurs
q: what is an innocent murmur
how do I tell innocent from pathologic murmurs
does a low grade mean a murmur is innocent
cards.x:
These are three groups of murmur, sorted by cause.

- Innocent: no physiologic or structural abnormality, usually from increased flow. Grade 1 to 3 of 6, and it diminishes when the patient stands, sits up or does a Valsalva maneuver. Most common in infancy and childhood, though healthy adults can have them too.
- Physiologic: from physiologic changes in body metabolism. Examples are anemia, pregnancy, fever and hyperthyroidism.
- Pathologic: from a structural abnormality of the heart or great vessels. Examples are aortic stenosis, pulmonic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and atrial septal defect.

Innocent is defined by the absence of symptoms and of any structural abnormality, not by the grade. A grade 1 to 3 murmur is not automatically innocent, and a murmur with a thrill is not innocent and needs working up. A murmur that appears in pregnancy is still worked up, even if it later proves physiologic.

cards.t: Document what you hear, not the disease name
k: the sound is not the diagnosis
how to write a murmur in the physical exam
q: how do I document a murmur
should I write aortic stenosis murmur in the exam
what is the difference between a finding and a diagnosis
cards.x:
The sound is not the diagnosis. In the physical examination section you document what you hear, where and when. You name the disease later, in the assessment.

So you would not write 'I hear an aortic stenosis murmur at the right second intercostal space.' You would write something like: a grade 4 of 6 systolic murmur, loudest at the right second intercostal space. Add that it radiates throughout the precordium, with greater intensity to the carotids, plus the thrill and where it was felt. Or: a systolic ejection murmur, crescendo-decrescendo, with its grade out of six filled in, radiating to the carotids.

The same goes for mitral stenosis. The exam line is a diastolic opening snap followed by a decrescendo murmur, best heard at the left fifth midclavicular line. 'Suspect mitral stenosis' belongs only in the differential, and an echocardiogram is what decides it.

Murmurs are findings that tell you something, and it is your job to hunt down what.

cards.t: How children differ: murmurs and splitting of the second heart sound
q: why do children have more murmurs
do the murmur rules apply to children
how is S2 splitting different in kids
cards.x:
Children break the usual rules. Their heart rate varies more with breathing. The physiologic splitting of the second heart sound is more pronounced. Blood also flows turbulently across normal valves, which is why a child can have a harmless (innocent) murmur.

That fits the innocent murmur, which is most common in infancy and childhood.

cards.t: Why systolic and diastolic murmurs come from different valve problems
k: which valve problems cause systolic murmurs
q: which valve lesions cause systolic murmurs
which valve lesions cause diastolic murmurs
are diastolic murmurs more serious
cards.x:
You can work out each murmur from which valves should be open and shut. In systole the aortic and pulmonic valves should be open and the mitral and tricuspid shut. So a systolic murmur often comes from a narrowed outflow valve (aortic or pulmonic stenosis) or a leaking inflow valve (mitral or tricuspid regurgitation). A muscle problem such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can also cause one.

In diastole it is the reverse. The mitral and tricuspid valves should be open and the aortic and pulmonic shut. So a diastolic murmur is either a leaking outflow valve (aortic or pulmonic regurgitation) or a narrowed inflow valve (mitral or tricuspid stenosis).

Diastolic murmurs are less common and harder to hear than systolic ones. They are more often pathologic.

cards.t: Pansystolic (holosystolic) murmurs
q: what is a holosystolic murmur
why are holosystolic murmurs always pathologic
which murmurs are holosystolic
cards.x:
A pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur begins with the first heart sound and continues all the way to the second. Something stays open through the whole of systole, so blood flows from a high-pressure chamber to a lower-pressure one through a structure that should be closed.

All pansystolic murmurs are pathologic. The two to know are mitral regurgitation, loudest at the apex, and tricuspid regurgitation, loudest at the lower left sternal border.

cards.t: Aortic stenosis murmur
q: what does the aortic stenosis murmur sound like
where does aortic stenosis radiate
how do I make aortic stenosis louder
cards.x:
Aortic stenosis is thickened aortic valve leaflets that open only to a narrow slit. Forward flow in systole has to be forced through that gap, which is why the murmur is midsystolic and harsh.

It is a medium-pitched, harsh, crescendo-decrescendo murmur loudest at the aortic area. It often radiates to the carotids, down the left sternal border and even to the apex. It can be soft or loud, with a thrill at grade 4 of 6 or above. It is heard better with the patient sitting and leaning forward, and it increases with squatting from standing and with leg raise.

Aortic stenosis is the one you will meet most often in practice. When a patient has a known murmur or a mechanical valve, spend time listening and feeling for the thrill.

cards.t: Pulmonic stenosis murmur
q: what does pulmonic stenosis sound like
where is pulmonic stenosis heard
how is pulmonic stenosis different from aortic stenosis
cards.x:
Pulmonic stenosis is the same obstruction as aortic stenosis but on the right side, at the pulmonic valve. It causes a right ventricular pressure load, with a thickened right ventricular wall.

The murmur is midsystolic, medium-pitched, harsh and crescendo-decrescendo, loudest at the pulmonic area. It can be soft to loud. If it is loud, there is a thrill, and it radiates toward the left shoulder and neck.

Quick way to tell it from aortic stenosis: look at where it is loudest and where it goes. Pulmonic stenosis is loudest at the pulmonic area and heads toward the left shoulder and neck. Aortic stenosis is loudest at the aortic area and heads to the carotids.

cards.t: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy murmur
q: what is hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
where is the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur heard
why is this murmur important
cards.x:
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is a disease of abnormally thickened heart muscle, most commonly the interventricular septum, with the muscle fibers not aligned properly. It is a muscle problem rather than a valve one. So the murmur is usually loudest along the left sternal border (Erb's point and the tricuspid area), not over the aortic area, and it usually does not radiate to the neck. It is a crescendo-decrescendo, midsystolic murmur that spreads down the left sternal border toward the apex.

Learn it so you do not sign off incorrectly on a sports physical. It is a bigger worry than the other ejection murmurs. Aortic stenosis and pulmonic stenosis worry you once they reach a certain point, but with this one you are worried, period. Take an 18-year-old whose brother has the disease and whose murmur gets louder with Valsalva. He is sent for an echocardiogram and kept from activity until it is done.

The thick septum narrows the outflow tract, and an emptier ventricle narrows it more. So the murmur increases with Valsalva and standing and decreases with squatting.

cards.t: Mitral regurgitation versus tricuspid regurgitation murmurs
k: pansystolic murmur at lower left sternal border
q: how do I tell mitral regurgitation from tricuspid regurgitation
does mitral regurgitation radiate to the axilla
where is tricuspid regurgitation loudest
cards.x:
Both are pansystolic murmurs from a valve that leaks backward through the whole of systole, and their radiation across the chest overlaps. Finding the spot where each is loudest is the key, and then the axilla.

- Mitral regurgitation: loudest at the apex, medium to high pitched and harsh, because the left ventricle is powerful and drives blood back into the left atrium. It radiates to the left axilla. It can be soft to loud, with an apical thrill if loud.
- Tricuspid regurgitation: loudest at the lower left sternal border, medium pitched and blowing, with a plateau shape. It radiates to the right sternum, xiphoid and left midclavicular line, but not to the axilla. It may increase slightly with inspiration.

So the quick way to tell them apart is location plus the axilla: mitral regurgitation radiates to the axilla and tricuspid regurgitation does not.

cards.t: Aortic regurgitation murmur
q: what does aortic regurgitation sound like
how do I listen for aortic regurgitation
why can aortic regurgitation be mistaken for breath sounds
cards.x:
In aortic regurgitation the aortic valve fails to close, so blood falls back into the left ventricle as soon as diastole begins. That gives an early diastolic, decrescendo murmur.

It is high pitched and blowing, which is why it can be mistaken for breath sounds. It is grade 1 to 3 and heard at the aortic area and down the left intercostal spaces. If it is loud it radiates to the apex.

To bring it out, sit the patient up, leaning forward, and have them hold their breath after exhaling.

cards.t: Pulmonic regurgitation murmur
k: early diastolic murmur at the pulmonic area
q: what does pulmonic regurgitation sound like
where is pulmonic regurgitation heard
how is pulmonic regurgitation different from aortic regurgitation
cards.x:
Pulmonic regurgitation is the same early diastolic leak as aortic regurgitation, but on the right side, heard over the pulmonic area. It is a high-pitched decrescendo murmur, grade 1 to 3, that may increase with inspiration. It does not radiate.

Quick way to tell it from aortic regurgitation: both are early diastolic, high-pitched decrescendo murmurs. Pulmonic regurgitation sits at the pulmonic area and has no radiation. Aortic regurgitation sits at the aortic area and radiates to the apex if loud.

cards.t: Mitral stenosis murmur
q: what does mitral stenosis sound like
how do I listen for mitral stenosis
why is the mitral stenosis murmur a rumble
cards.x:
In mitral stenosis the mitral valve is narrowed, so it has to be forced open in diastole: first the snap as it opens, then a low rumble as blood squeezes through the narrow valve.

The murmur is a low-pitched, decrescendo rumble, mid to late diastolic, grade 1 to 4, with little or no radiation. It is loudest at the apex. Use the bell, at the apex, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.

The sequence is the snap of the valve opening, then the rumble, so the murmur follows the opening snap.

cards.t: Tricuspid stenosis murmur
q: what does tricuspid stenosis sound like
where is tricuspid stenosis heard
how is tricuspid stenosis different from mitral stenosis
cards.x:
Tricuspid stenosis is the same diastolic obstruction as mitral stenosis, but on the right side. The murmur is mid to late diastolic, decrescendo, grade 1 to 4, a low-pitched rumble best heard with the bell, with little or no radiation.

Quick way to tell it from mitral stenosis: location. Tricuspid stenosis is heard at the lower left sternal border, near the xiphoid, while mitral stenosis is heard at the apex.

cards.t: Pericardial friction rub
q: what is a pericardial friction rub
what does a friction rub sound like
how do I bring out a pericardial friction rub
cards.x:
A pericardial friction rub comes from inflammation of the pericardial sac (pericarditis). Normally the visceral and parietal layers of the pericardium glide silently over each other. When they are inflamed, they rub with every beat.

It is a scratchy, scraping noise heard intermittently through both diastole and systole. Intensity varies and the pitch is high, so use the diaphragm. It has a plateau shape, is most often heard at Erb's point, and has little radiation.

It may increase when the patient leans forward, exhales and holds their breath, which is the same position used to bring out aortic regurgitation.

cards.t: The Valsalva maneuver and what it does to murmurs
q: how is the Valsalva maneuver done
what does Valsalva do to a murmur
how does Valsalva change mitral valve prolapse
cards.x:
The Valsalva maneuver, or strain, is a forceful expiration against a closed airway. The supine patient bears down, or pushes against your hand on the mid-abdomen.

This raises the pressure inside the chest and decreases left ventricular filling, so preload falls. The heart is emptier, and that changes the murmurs:

- Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur: increases.
- Aortic stenosis murmur: gets softer or does not change.
- Mitral valve prolapse: the click comes earlier and the murmur lengthens.

Releasing the strain does the opposite: the release phase of Valsalva fills the left ventricle again, much like squatting does. Standing quickly from a squat, which also decreases filling, gives the same pattern of changes as the strain phase.

cards.t: Standing, squatting and leg raise: preload maneuvers
q: what does standing do to a murmur
why does squatting make aortic stenosis louder
what do I do if a patient cannot squat
cards.x:
These maneuvers change how much blood returns to the heart.

Standing quickly from squatting: blood moves to the legs, so less returns to the heart and left ventricular preload falls. The hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur becomes louder, the aortic stenosis murmur gets softer, and in mitral valve prolapse the click comes earlier and the murmur lengthens.

Squatting from standing, or a leg raise: blood stored in the legs returns, so venous return and preload increase. The hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur gets softer, because the outflow obstruction lessens. The aortic stenosis murmur gets louder, because more blood rushes past the narrow valve. In mitral valve prolapse the click moves later in systole and the murmur shortens.

Practical tips: the squat-and-stand maneuvers need you and the patient to move together. If a patient cannot squat, raise their legs instead.

cards.t: Isometric (sustained) hand grip and murmurs
q: what does hand grip do to murmurs
how do I do the hand grip maneuver
which murmurs get louder with hand grip
cards.x:
Sustained (isometric) hand grip means squeezing hard and holding, for example on a rolled-up shirt or a washcloth. It raises vascular resistance, which is more afterload: the heart has to pump against a higher pressure.

Two sets of findings go with it:

- It makes the aortic stenosis and the hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy murmurs softer.
- It increases the systolic murmurs of mitral regurgitation and ventricular septal defect, and the diastolic murmurs of aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis.

cards.t: Why hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and aortic stenosis respond opposite ways
k: why HOCM gets louder with standing
q: why does the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur get louder with Valsalva
why does the aortic stenosis murmur get louder with squatting
how do I tell aortic stenosis from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
One rule explains the whole hypertrophic cardiomyopathy row. Its obstruction is a thick septum narrowing the outflow tract, and a smaller ventricle narrows that tract even further. So anything that reduces filling (Valsalva, standing) makes the murmur louder, and anything that increases filling (squatting, leg raise) makes it softer.

Aortic stenosis runs the other way, because more blood through a fixed narrow valve makes more noise. More filling means more flow past the valve and a louder murmur; less filling means a softer one.

So the quick way to tell the two apart is to change the filling and watch the direction. Squatting fills the left ventricle: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy softens, aortic stenosis gets louder. Standing or straining empties it, and every one of those reverses.

cards.t: Positions that bring murmurs closer to the stethoscope
q: what position do I use for mitral stenosis
how do I listen for aortic regurgitation
why use the left lateral decubitus position
cards.x:
Some murmurs are best heard just by moving the patient so the heart sits closer to the stethoscope.

- Left lateral decubitus, for the apex: the third and fourth heart sounds and mitral stenosis. Lower the head of the bed, turn the patient to the left, and reach over them.
- Seated, leaning forward, exhaling completely and holding, for listening along the sternal border: aortic regurgitation and the pericardial friction rub.

Maneuvers go a step further than positions. They change filling and resistance, so murmurs that sound alike can be told apart. Above all, they separate the murmurs of mitral valve prolapse and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy from aortic stenosis.

cards.t: Chronic arterial insufficiency: what you see and why
q: what are the signs of chronic arterial insufficiency
why do arterial ulcers occur on the toes
why is the leg hairless in arterial insufficiency
cards.x:
Chronic arterial insufficiency is a long-term shortage of arterial blood reaching the limb, and most of the findings follow from that.

- Pain with walking (claudication), like angina of the legs, which can progress to pain at rest.
- The limb is cool to touch, pale or dusky red, with foot pallor on elevation and dusky rubor on dependency. There is no edema.
- The skin is thin and shiny with loss of hair. Poor supply starves what the body needs least to survive, so hair loss and thin, shiny skin are common findings.
- Pulses are decreased.
- The ulcer is at the distal toes, the most poorly perfused point. It is painful unless neuropathy has taken the sensation away.
- Gangrene may develop.

cards.t: Chronic venous insufficiency: what you see and why
q: what are the signs of chronic venous insufficiency
why is there pitting edema in venous insufficiency
how do I tell arterial from venous insufficiency
cards.x:
Chronic venous insufficiency is a long-term failure of the veins to return blood from the legs. The problem is not blood getting down into the leg. It is blood getting back up out of it. So fluid pools distally, stretches the skin until it breaks down, and stains it brown.

- Pain: usually none or mild, an ache or heaviness that eases with elevation, unlike claudication. Temperature: normal.
- Pitting edema is present. The skin is thickened, with stasis dermatitis, purpura and varicosities.
- Color is cyanotic or brownish pigmentation (hemosiderin staining), with cyanosis of the foot when dependent.
- The ulcer is around the ankles, over the medial and lateral malleolus. It is small, painful, with granulation tissue and fibrin and irregular borders.
- Gangrene is rare. Pulses are normal, although heavy edema over the foot can make them hard to feel. A small Doppler probe will find them.

Quick way to tell it from arterial insufficiency: venous has edema, normal temperature and pulses, and ulcers at the ankle. Arterial has cool skin, no edema, decreased pulses and ulcers at the toes.

cards.t: Inspecting the extremities and capillary refill
q: how do I check capillary refill
what should I inspect on the extremities
what is Quincke's pulse
cards.x:
Start the peripheral vascular examination by looking. Inspect the upper and lower extremities for size, symmetry, venous pattern, hair growth pattern and edema. Check skin color for erythema, cyanosis, jaundice, pigmentation changes and ulceration, and look for skin thickening and varicosities (mild to severe dilatation of veins, mainly in the lower extremities).

Always compare one extremity with the other: is the swelling unilateral or bilateral? Note relative size and the prominence of veins, tendons and bones. Unilateral findings, especially arterial ones, may need urgent work-up.

For capillary refill, press on the fingernail, release, and time the return of pink; it should take 2 to 3 seconds. Quincke's pulse is a related sign: after the pressure is released, the capillary bed flashes red to pale with each heartbeat.

cards.t: Grading pulses and what an absent pulse means
q: how do I grade a pulse
what causes absent pulses
can a pulse be hard to feel but still present
cards.x:
Grade the amplitude of every pulse and always compare both sides. From strongest to weakest the descriptions are bounding, increased, brisk (normal), faint or diminished, and absent.

Absent pulses may suggest an arterial disorder from atherosclerosis or systemic embolism. Also consider small vessel disease such as diabetes mellitus.

A pulse that is hard to feel is not necessarily absent. Pulses may be hard to feel in patients who are obese or muscular. With heavy edema over the foot, the pulses can be hard to feel even though they are normal. A small Doppler probe will find them.

cards.t: Where to feel the carotid, brachial, radial and ulnar pulses
q: where is the brachial pulse
how do I palpate the carotid pulse
why can't I feel the ulnar pulse
cards.x:
Each pulse has a spot.

- Carotid: lateral to the trachea. Ask the patient to hold their breath, auscultate before palpating, and palpate one side at a time.
- Brachial: medial to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa.
- Radial: the lateral portion of the wrist, on the thumb side.
- Ulnar: the medial wrist, deep on the flexor surface. Partly flexing the wrist helps, and a normal ulnar pulse may not be palpable at all.

Always compare the two sides. The carotid is listened to first and felt one side at a time.

cards.t: Where to feel the femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
q: where is the femoral pulse
how do I feel the popliteal pulse
where is the dorsalis pedis pulse
cards.x:
Leg pulses have their own spots.

- Femoral: below the inguinal ligament, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.
- Popliteal: harder to feel and may not be felt. That is not an issue if the pulses beyond it are present. Press the fingertips deep into the midline of the fossa with the knee flexed and relaxed. Or have the patient prone with the knee at 90 degrees and press the thumbs deep.
- Dorsalis pedis: on the top of the foot, lateral to the extensor tendon of the great toe.
- Posterior tibial: behind the medial malleolus.

Grade each and compare both sides.

cards.t: Radial-femoral pulse lag (coarctation of the aorta)
q: what is pulse lag
how do I check for radial-femoral delay
what does a delayed femoral pulse mean
cards.x: Pulse lag is a delay between two pulses that should arrive together. To test for it, feel the radial and femoral pulses at the same time. A femoral pulse that arrives after the radial pulse suggests coarctation of the aorta.

cards.t: Palpating the abdominal aorta
q: how do I palpate the abdominal aorta
what am I looking for when feeling the aorta
where do I press to feel the aorta
cards.x: To palpate the abdominal aorta, press deeply with both hands in the upper abdomen. You are looking for its size, meaning how wide it is. That matters whether or not it is easy to feel. The companion step is listening over the abdomen for a bruit at the aorta, which is a sound of vascular origin.

cards.t: Bruits: where to listen and what they mean
q: where do I listen for bruits
what does a bruit mean
how far from the aorta is the renal artery listening site
cards.x:
A bruit is a murmur-like sound of vascular rather than cardiac origin. Listen at four places:

- Aorta: midline of the abdomen, above the umbilicus.
- Renal: 3 to 4 cm lateral to the aorta.
- Iliac: 3 to 4 cm lateral to the umbilicus and about 2 cm inferior.
- Femoral: directly over the femoral artery, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.

A bruit often means narrowing, and so possible arterial insufficiency of whatever that vessel supplies, though turbulent flow can have other causes. For example, a renal bruit raises the question of whether the kidneys are getting enough blood.

cards.t: Allen test
q: how is the Allen test done
what does the Allen test check
why do an Allen test before an arterial blood gas
cards.x:
The Allen test evaluates the arterial supply of the hand by checking the patency of the radial and ulnar arteries.

1. Compress both the radial and the ulnar artery.
2. Ask the patient to clench the fist for 30 seconds.
3. With both arteries still occluded, ask the patient to open the fist. The hand is pale.
4. Release the ulnar artery and watch the hand fill; that tests the patency of the ulnar artery.
5. Repeat, releasing the radial artery, to test its patency.

Normally the pink returns promptly. Pallor that persists means that artery is occluded. It is done before drawing an arterial blood gas, to be sure the ulnar artery can supply the hand if the radial artery is injured.

cards.t: Ankle brachial index: what it is and how it is measured
q: what is the ankle brachial index
how is the ankle brachial index calculated
how do I measure the ankle brachial index
cards.x:
The ankle brachial index compares blood pressure in the foot with blood pressure in the arm, calculated for each leg. Take the higher of the two ankle pressures (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial) on that side. Divide it by the higher brachial systolic pressure, and record the result to two decimal places. It is accurate at detecting the fall in pressure beyond an arterial stenosis (narrowing). So it is used to assess peripheral arterial disease: pain, claudication, numbness, weakness, weak or absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, and distal pallor.

To measure the arm pressure, the patient lies supine and rests for 10 minutes. Put the cuff on the arm and an ultrasound (Doppler) probe over the brachial pulse. Inflate to 20 mm Hg above the last audible pulse. Deflate slowly (about 1 mm Hg per second), and record the pressure at which the pulse becomes audible again. Take two measurements in each arm and average them. For the ankle, put the cuff just above the malleoli and find the dorsalis pedis with the Doppler. Repeat over the posterior tibial, then do the other leg.

cards.t: Interpreting the ankle brachial index
q: what is a normal ankle brachial index
what ankle brachial index suggests peripheral arterial disease
what does an ankle brachial index over 1.40 mean
cards.x:
The ankle brachial index is read against fixed ranges. A low number means the pressure in the foot has fallen below the pressure in the arm, which is what happens beyond a narrowed artery.

- Over 1.40: suggests a noncompressible, calcified vessel.
- 0.90 to 1.40: normal.
- Under 0.90: suggestive of peripheral arterial disease.
- Under 0.50: suggests severe peripheral arterial disease.

Use the exact cutoffs (0.90 to 1.40 normal, under 0.90 abnormal) rather than rounding to "1". The index is a test for chronic arterial disease, such as claudication or toe ulcers that will not heal. For a suspected acute blockage or embolus this index is not the right test; a computed tomography angiogram is the imaging suggested instead.

cards.t: Homans sign for deep vein thrombosis
q: how do I do the Homans sign
what is a positive Homans sign
does a negative Homans sign rule out a clot
cards.x:
Homans sign is a test for deep vein thrombosis. Classically you quickly dorsiflex the foot at the ankle with the knee bent. It is positive if the patient has pain behind the knee. But the sign is now considered unreliable. It should not be used alone to decide whether a clot is present.

A negative result does not reassure you. Perform it when you already suspect a deep vein thrombosis, on the leg you are worried about. Do not use it as a screening rule-out. Picture one patient with unilateral leg swelling after a long flight who is also a smoker on birth control and has a recently injured ankle. If the test is positive, it fits your suspicion but does not prove a clot. The diagnosis still needs a probability score, D-dimer and ultrasound. If it is negative, you are still worried.

cards.t: Pitting edema: what it is and how to check for it
q: how do I check for pitting edema
where do I press to test for pitting
is edema always vascular
cards.x:
Edema is excessive fluid in the extravascular interstitial space. Up to 10% of body weight can accumulate before pitting appears. On inspection it obscures veins, tendons and bony prominences. Always compare sides: is it unilateral or bilateral?

Pitting is the depression left by the pressure of your thumb. Press firmly for at least 2 seconds over the dorsum of the foot, behind the medial malleolus, or over the shins. These sites have bone beneath, so there is something to press against. Then describe both the depth (the grade) and the extent, meaning how far up the edema reaches. Edema can also be non-pitting.

Edema is not always a vascular finding: heart failure produces it with healthy vessels. Venous stasis edema classically sits from the knee down. It is often in one leg or comes with brown staining and varicose veins. That pattern points to the veins, although heart failure can also cause leg edema.

cards.t: Pitting edema grades 0+ to 4+
q: how is pitting edema graded
what is 3+ pitting edema
how deep is 2+ pitting
cards.x:
Pitting edema is graded by how deep the pit is and how long it lasts. Every step is 2 mm deeper.

- 0+: no pitting edema.
- 1+: 2 mm, mild; the depression disappears rapidly.
- 2+: 4 mm, moderate; disappears in 10 to 15 seconds.
- 3+: 6 mm, moderately severe; may last more than 1 minute.
- 4+: 8 mm, severe; can last more than 2 minutes.

So when you press and release, watch the depth of the pit and time how long it takes to fill back in.

cards.t: Order and set-up of the cardiovascular examination
q: what is the order of the cardiovascular examination
how should I position the patient
what equipment do I need for a cardiovascular exam
cards.x:
The order is inspection, palpation, auscultation, then special techniques. Inspection includes measuring the jugular venous pressure: look for the pulsation while you inspect the neck and carotids, and measure its highest point.

Equipment: a stethoscope, plus a ruler, penlight and tongue depressor for the vascular findings. Use enough light and exposure, with tangential lighting during inspection so every contour shows. Keep the room quiet, your hands warm and your nails short.

The patient is in a gown, and the examination is never done over clothing. Remember positioning: supine at about 30 to 45 degrees, left lateral decubitus, and seated and leaning forward. With a reluctant patient, offer to place the stethoscope under the gown while it stays covered; the aim is nothing between the stethoscope and the skin. If a patient refuses, do not examine them; document it thoroughly.

cards.t: Complete versus focused cardiovascular examination
q: what is the difference between a complete and a focused cardiovascular exam
how do I choose maneuvers for a focused exam
what does a complete cardiac exam include
cards.x:
A complete cardiovascular examination runs everything. That means the precordium (the chest wall over the heart) in every area, with both the diaphragm and the bell. It also means the extra sounds and the peripheral vascular examination from head to toe.

A focused examination keeps the same order and technique but chooses. You pick the areas and positions that match the complaint. You pick the maneuvers that answer the question you have, rather than doing every one.
